html:
A Byzantine church of the Virgin "All-Blessed" (Pammakaristos) in the Çarşamba quarter of old Istanbul, now the Fethiye Mosque. Most scholars date it to the 11th or 12th century; many credit it to the emperor Michael VII Doukas (1071 to 1078). Shortly after 1310 Martha Glabas added a side chapel, the parekklesion, as a memorial to her husband Michael Glabas Tarchaneiotes, a general of Andronikos II. A verse inscription by the court poet Manuel Philes runs round the chapel inside and out.

After the fall of Constantinople the Orthodox patriarchs moved from Hagia Sophia to the Holy Apostles and then, in 1456, here, where they stayed until 1587; a synod held here in 1484 rejected the union with Rome agreed at the Council of Florence. Around 1591 Sultan Murad III made it a mosque, named Fethiye, "of the conquest", for his conquests in Georgia and Azerbaijan. The builders tore out the inner arcades and the three apses and added a domed hall set at an angle to the old church.

The parekklesion kept its Byzantine form: a small cross-in-square chapel with five domes, built in the Palaiologan style. Its mosaics, after those of Hagia Sophia and the Chora the largest group of Byzantine mosaics in the city, show Christ Pantocrator in the dome ringed by twelve Old Testament prophets, Christ with the Virgin and John the Baptist in the apse, and the Baptism of Christ. The Byzantine Institute of America and Dumbarton Oaks restored it in 1949, and the chapel has been a museum since. The main building is still a mosque.
